newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: CBA head warns of savings and loans risk.
newsitem.headline: CBA head warns of savings and loans risk.

text.p: Commonwealth Bank of Australia (CBA) managing director David Murray on Wednedsday attacked the Wallis Financial System Inquiry's plan to shake up prudential supervision, saying it would take Australia into uncharted waters.
Murray described the inquiry's findings regarding prudential supervision as similiar to those of the United States' savings and loans system.
Murray told a Committee for Economic Development of Australia (CEDA) function that Wallis' plan to treat all deposit taking institutions in similar ways prudentially posed a number of risks.

Murray said Wallis' plan to strip the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) of its supervisory powers would put the RBA in a difficult position because it would continue to have responsibility for the safety of the system.

"Wallis should be lauded in terms of opening up competition but (the prudential proposals) do take us into uncharted waters which set up for Australia a savings and loans system that cost the citizens of the United States an awful lot of money," Murray said.
He said he disagreed with the creation of a savings and loans system, which regulates non-banks and banks in the same way.

Murray also said he was concerned about the levels of disclosure proposed by Wallis and he wanted savers to know that money put into asset management vehicles like unit trusts and managed funds were not as safe as bank savings accounts.
"I'm very concerned that the statements of disclosure run from deposit taking institutions into asset management vehicles," he said.
Any disclosure must make clear when a customer's savings are drifting from the area of deposits into asset management vehicles.
"If we don't keep a separation we will suffer as a community when the hurt comes, and it always will, because the system goes through cycles," Murray said.
Murray said he was also concerned that Wallis had not addressed the need to keep financial services affordable and efficient for a majority of Australians at an acceptable cost.
The Wallis report, announced on April 9, recommended the creation of a single prudential regulator for the financial system known as the Australian Prudential Regulation Commission (APRC).
The APRC should be separate from but coordinate closely with the RBA, which itself should remain responsible for system stability and liquidity management.
Australian Treasurer Peter Costello is considering the recommendations of the Wallis report and is due to announce his decisions later this year.
